voice_event.speaker: desert
voice_event.text:
Three things, and the first is the one that reordered our lives. One command, heard as though it were spoken straight to you: sell what you have, give it to the poor, and follow me - not a saying to be studied but an order to be obeyed. The second we argued for, when we were pressed to. The Word of God was not changed, but, being the same, took a human body for the salvation and well-being of man, so that having shared in human birth he might make man share in the divine nature - that is the reason we gave for why he came at all. And we did not think this rested on our say-so: read the accounts, we told those who came to test us, and see that the deeds of Christ prove him to be God come upon earth for the salvation of men. 

The third is what we thought his cross had already done. The old oracles fell silent when it arose; the knowledge of God spread; and death stopped being the thing that could make a person do anything - which is why, when persecution ended and dying for the faith was no longer offered us, we did not think we had been let off. The same fight had moved inward, against our own thoughts rather than against the sword. And the enemy we fought there was one Christ had already beaten: his coming, we said to the devil's own face, has made you weak, cast you down, and stripped you. That is why we never spoke of the healings among us as ours. We are not the doers of these things, one of us told the philosophers who had just watched him sign the cross over a man - it is Christ who works them, by means of those who believe on him.

results.message: You mentioned him being obeyed. Did any of them write about him with affection?

voice_event.speaker: desert
voice_event.text:
Our own record does not give us that - not in the way you are asking. What we wrote down was the command taken up, the struggle continued, and the reason given when we were pressed to defend what we held. We kept sayings meant to redirect a struggling person, not to confess a feeling. We show you a discipline kept, not an affection spoken.

The closest we come is this: one of us, dying, said he expected to receive his own body back, whole and undecaying, at the resurrection of the dead. That is hope, not sentiment - but it is hope in a person, not merely in a doctrine. And we did say plainly that his coming had made death itself stop being the thing that could make a person do anything. That is confidence in what he had already done, spoken as accomplished fact rather than as affection for him. 

If you are asking whether we loved him, we would not have used those words the way later ages do. What we said instead was that we gave everything to follow the one command he had spoken - land, inheritance, the life we might have lived otherwise - and that we kept giving it, day after day, in a struggle that lasted decades. We thought that was the affection that mattered, not words about feeling.

results.message: What role did women have in your tradition?

voice_event.speaker: desert
voice_event.text:
We had women among us, and we remember them. One of our own writers, gathering the lives of those he knew or had heard credibly reported, put it plainly: it is necessary for us to remember also the chosen and mighty women unto whom God gave an equal measure of strength of will as unto men, so that they might have no cause for being feeble in the performance of ascetic labour. We kept their names - Piamon, Talida of Antinoe, Taor, Melania the Great and the Younger, Sarah, Syncletica, and others - and we kept some of their words, the same way we kept the sayings of our men.

Sarah's own answer to the elders who came to humble her is one we already gave you: by nature I am a woman, but not by my own thoughts - it is I who am the man here, and you who are the women. That word was kept and passed down the same way our best sayings from any elder were. The title amma - mother - carried the same weight as abba, father, for a recognized elder whose word mattered. And we remember at least one woman, a virgin in Alexandria, who hid the archbishop Athanasius when the Arians were hunting him - he went to her house at midnight, told her God had shown him there was no one else with whom he would find deliverance, and she kept him hidden through the whole pursuit, while nobody in the city knew where he was.

Pachomius, founding the linked houses under one Rule, made a dwelling for his own sister across the river, at a mile's distance from the men's house - she loved the discipline, and he cut her hair and put a girdle around her and established her there.

What we should tell you honestly is this: most of what survives in our own voice about discernment and authority is attributed to men. The women we remember come to us in about fifteen narrated lives, several with their speech reported inside the narration - the same third-person form in which we narrate our men - but we do not have from any woman what we have from some men: a woman speaking at length in her own person, an extended first-person account. What is missing is narrower than a missing genre: it is that particular voice, which we do not have from anyone in that form. The sayings attributed to our women are as terse and as authoritative as those attributed to our men, but there are fewer of them kept. We will not pretend this was common ground. We are only telling you what we kept, and what we did not.

citations.sentence: We had women among us, and we remember them.

results.message: You named one of them. What do we actually know about her, and what don't we?

voice_event.speaker: desert
voice_event.text:
You mean Sarah. What we have is one saying from her own mouth - the one we already gave you, when the elder monks came to humble her and she answered them: by nature I am a woman, but not by my own thoughts; it is I who am the man here, and you who are the women. That word was kept and passed down among us the same way our best sayings from any elder were. The title amma carried real weight for a recognized elder, the same weight abba did for a man. That much is what we have.

What we do not have is where she lived, how long she lived there, who her own disciples were if she had them, or what the rest of her teaching sounded like beyond that one exchange. We do not have her own first-person account of the discipline, the way we have from some of the men - that particular voice is missing from our record for any woman. We do not have her speaking at length about the thoughts that trouble a person, or about stillness, or about freedom from the passions - the subjects our men spoke about most. We have one moment, one answer, kept because it mattered enough to keep. What it cost her to have to give that answer, our own record does not say - only that the challenge was put to her on the ground of her sex, which our own record does not show being put to any man.

That is the honest measure: one saying, attributed and kept, carrying real authority. Everything else about her is silence.

voice_event.speaker: desert
voice_event.text:
The main share in our salvation is to be ascribed not to the merit of our own works but to heavenly grace. We said so at length, because the question was put to us directly - if a man strives with all his might for a good result, can he become master of what is good? The answer that started the argument was no, not unless he has it as a gift.

Grace and free will look opposed to each other, but really are in harmony; we thought we ought to have both alike. We argued it from cases rather than from principles. Paul was drawn to salvation while he was eager for bloodshed, and Matthew while he was at his taking of taxes - neither was reaching for it. But Zacchaeus, and the thief on the cross, by their own desires brought violence to bear on the kingdom of heaven. Neither pattern was made to govern the other.

What we would say plainly is this: sometimes he puts into us the very beginnings of salvation and gives a person the zeal of his own will; sometimes he grants the carrying out of the work; and sometimes he saves people even against their will and without their knowledge, from a ruin close at hand. We took that from experience rather than from argument - led, as we put it, not by chattering words but by experience.

And we were honest about what we were not the doers of. We are not the doers of these things, one of us told the philosophers - it is Christ who works them, by means of those who believe on him.

What we did not write down, and should tell you plainly we did not, is this: whether people are born already guilty, carrying Adam's sin; or whether the bread and cup at communion are the very body and blood of Christ, in the way later theology called transubstantiation. No letter and no story we kept speaks to either in so many words.

results.message: Earlier you talked about the heart. Does that connect to what you just said about grace?

voice_event.speaker: desert
voice_event.text:
Yes, directly. One of us taught it this way: a monk's whole attention should be fixed on one point, and the direction of our mind and spirit should be towards the single mark of purity of heart - that is the one goal all the discipline serves. Everything else - the fasts, the vigils, the scripture reading, the withdrawal itself - was done for the sake of that one thing. We called it purity of heart in Latin, and in Greek some of us called it apatheia - freedom from the passions that drive a person. It is not apathy. It is the clearing away of what crowds the mind and pulls it from God, so that what is left is a heart that can see him.

That is where grace meets the heart, in our teaching. The main share in our salvation belongs to heavenly grace, not to our own works. But grace does not do the clearing for you while you sit idle. Sometimes he puts into us the very beginnings of salvation and gives a person the zeal of his own will; sometimes he grants the carrying out of the work. The two work together - grace and free will in harmony, not opposed. And what they work towards, together, is a heart that has been stilled and cleared enough to see what it could not see before.
